findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify how step-4 resume distinguishes a pause this repair NEWLY WROTE (clear it) from a same-reason pause it merely OBSERVED already present (leave it), e.g. a repair-unique pause reason plus verifying set_pause returned a newly-created OID before clear_gate runs, so the finally never resumes an operator/prior pause the repair did not own.
evidence: Plan step 4: 'Clear only the pause written/observed by this repair in finally'
src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/_ref_lock.py:696-697 set_pause returns the existing OID (no write) when reason matches: 'elif existing["reason"] == reason: return old'
src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/_ref_lock.py:634-639 clear_gate deletes by observed OID, reason-agnostic and idempotent
The plan gives no reason-uniqueness scheme or wrote-new sentinel to gate the clear
findings.finding: The repair sequence's step-4 resume ('Clear only the pause written/observed by this repair') does not distinguish a pause this repair NEWLY WROTE from a same-reason pause it merely OBSERVED. set_pause() is idempotent on an identical reason (returns the existing OID without writing), and clear_gate() deletes the gate ref by observed OID regardless of who authored it. So if an operator (or an interrupted prior repair) already holds a same-reason pause when the scheduled repair runs, step 1 is a no-op and the step-4 finally clear_gate would resume a pause the repair never owned — silently reopening a bridge intended to stay paused.
findings.location: Portable destructive-repair control — repair sequence steps 1 and 4
scenarios: Operator pauses the bridge with the same reason string the scheduled repair uses, then a scheduled fsck --repair runs and completes: its finally clears the operator's pause
A prior repair crashed leaving its pause in place; the retry repair observes (not writes) it and then clears it in finally even though its own body aborted early
findings.suggested_fix: Have the repair use a repair-unique pause reason and record whether step 1's set_pause actually created a new ref (new OID != the pre-observed OID); only clear in finally when this repair created the pause, otherwise leave the observed pause untouched.

findings.checklist_item: Realign GitLab scope with the parent epic 2f79-2b32-28c5-4eb3: either restore the parent's GitLab Portability deliverables (five-env matrix incl. gitlab, committed .gitlab-ci.yml, vendored-schema offline validation, three-config exit/secret/timeout cross-check and three-config shellcheck) into this leaf or an explicitly-named sibling, or first amend the parent to remove GitLab from its ACs and its 'not as future adopter work' rule — do not silently re-scope GitLab out at the leaf.
evidence: Leaf: 'GitLab is also out of scope. There is no current .gitlab-ci.yml, runner, or consumer... no unrun GitLab config or schema validator ships here.'
Leaf narrows the parent's five-environment matrix to four: 'representative local, GitHub Actions, Jenkins, and bare environments' and 'scrubbed local/GHA/Jenkins/bare environments'.
Parent AC: 'A contract test runs the entrypoint under scrubbed environments for {local, github-actions, jenkins, gitlab, bare} and passes identically'.
Parent AC: '`Jenkinsfile` and `.gitlab-ci.yml` exist as REAL COMMITTED FILES that the docs reference rather than duplicate'.
Parent AC: 'All three configs are asserted to share one exit-code table, one secret-name set, and one timeout' — leaf reduces this to 'both provider wrappers'.
Parent AC: '.gitlab-ci.yml validates against GitLab's official JSON schema, offline... the SCHEMA DOCUMENT... is VENDORED into the repo at a pinned version' — leaf ships no such validator.
Parent AC: 'shellcheck runs over script bodies extracted from all three configs' — leaf extracts only GHA and Jenkins.

Parent constraint contradicted by the leaf's reframing: 'Uncovered risks are documented as KNOWN GAPS outside the AC, not as future adopter work' — the leaf's 'accepted follow-up only when a real consumer exists' is precisely the prohibited future-adopter framing.

No sibling carve-out is named as the GitLab/portability owner (the 4752-3afb split comment enumerates carve-outs c61a/4a44/e27c, none covering GitLab), and the leaf does not defer GitLab to a sibling; it re-scopes it out entirely.
findings.finding: The leaf declares GitLab out of scope, but the parent epic's Portability AC block makes GitLab an in-scope, in-session-verifiable deliverable, and explicitly forbids reframing uncovered work as future-adopter work — so the leaf steps outside the parent's contract rather than narrowing it.
findings.location: Plan 'Context' (GitLab-out-of-scope paragraph) and AC line 'GitLab support is an accepted follow-up only when a real consumer exists' vs. parent 2f79-2b32-28c5-4eb3 'Portability AC' block
scenarios: The parent epic is closed/verified while its GitLab Portability ACs (committed .gitlab-ci.yml, five-env matrix, vendored-schema validation, three-config cross-check, three-config shellcheck) were never delivered by any child.
A reviewer verifying the epic's 'verifiable in-session' guarantee finds the five-environment/three-config assertions unmet.

evidence: 1 criterion line(s) bundle multiple deliverables with 'and' (split so each is independently verifiable).
findings.suggested_fix: Split compound criteria, replace subjective terms with observable outcomes, and state how each is verified.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the entrypoint timeout value (or its derivation) so providers inherit it rather than each choosing one.
evidence: Plan states the entrypoint 'owns ... and timeout' and is 'the wrapper source of truth for the secret-name set and timeout' but never states a value or derivation
Unlike CANONICAL_EXIT_CODES (derived from _Disposition 0/1/2) and secret names, the timeout has no stated origin
findings.finding: The entrypoint is declared the source of truth for 'timeout' but the plan never states the timeout value or how it is chosen, leaving a defaultable design detail unspecified.
findings.location: Runner-neutral entrypoint section: 'owns the canonical wrapper contract (CANONICAL_EXIT_CODES, required environment names, and timeout)'
scenarios: Executor must pick an arbitrary timeout value and providers must not re-declare it
findings.suggested_fix: Name a concrete default timeout in scripts/run_reconcile_bridge.py (e.g. align to the existing 20-minute schedule) and have the contract test assert wrappers do not override it.

findings.finding: The plan's research premise materially undercounts rebar's GitHub coupling: it claims 'GITHUB_* appears three times, two in docstrings,' but src/rebar/mirror_guard.py hardcodes GITHUB_REPO='navapbc/rebar' (line 32), reads os.environ.get('GITHUB_TOKEN') (line 231), and calls api.github.com directly (lines 153,168,174), while llm/usage_log.py and llm/usage_report.py reference GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY. This is a real GitHub-coupled consumer outside the workflow wrapper that the 'the portability surface is the workflow wrapper, not the code' claim does not enumerate.
findings.location: Plan body: 'rebar's code is already essentially CI-neutral (... GITHUB_* appears three times, two in docstrings)'
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the 'three times, two in docstrings' claim with an accurate enumeration (mirror_guard.py GITHUB_REPO/GITHUB_TOKEN/api.github.com; usage_log/usage_report GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY) and state whether mirror_guard is intentionally excluded from AC #2/#4 or must route through the portable gate.

findings.finding: AC line 2 requires `_reconciler_pause` to use a 'portable gate' replacing the GitHub-specific `gh workflow disable/enable reconcile-bridge.yml`, but the plan never names the portable mechanism. Pausing a *scheduled* reconciler pass is intrinsically provider-specific: `gh workflow disable` pauses a GHA schedule, while Jenkins/GitLab schedule the reconciler on their own platform schedulers with no provider-neutral CLI or git operation that pauses a cron-scheduled job across all three. The one git-ref candidate (the leased CAS `refs/reconciler/lock`) is explicitly excluded by the very code the plan cites (fsck_repair.py:279-280: the lock 'is not the pause mechanism'). This is an asserted capability with a genuine capability gap and no named feasible mechanism, and it is not routed to a SPIKE.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria line 2: '`_reconciler_pause` uses the portable gate'; body para 1 (gh shell-out at fsck_repair.py:284,291)

findings.finding: The plan mandates a 'portable gate' replacing the gh-based `_reconciler_pause` but never specifies the replacement mechanism; `gh workflow disable` is intrinsically GitHub-specific (no cross-provider schedule-disable exists), and the code shows the destructive-repair safety actually rests on the already-portable CAS refs/reconciler/lock (`_reconciler_in_flight`), not the best-effort pause.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria: '`rebar` core requires no `gh` binary for any documented operation; `_reconciler_pause` uses the portable gate'
findings.suggested_fix: Name the CAS lock (`refs/reconciler/lock` / `_reconciler_in_flight`) as the portable gate and drop the best-effort schedule-disable, or define a provider-agnostic pause interface; add an AC that the destructive repair aborts fail-closed on an indeterminate lock regardless of provider.

findings.finding: The plan asserts a contract test runs shellcheck over script bodies extracted from all three configs (AC line 11), but shellcheck is an external non-Python binary and the plan does not state its availability precondition (unlike the GitLab-schema item, which explicitly scopes to 'dependencies rebar already has'). If shellcheck is absent from the test runner, the check either silently skips or errors — the same 'present command that silently lies' failure mode the plan's own det_lint prior-art warns about.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria line 11: 'shellcheck runs over script bodies extracted from all three configs and FAILS on an unparseable config'
